reason: Audited the whole iff proof. Forward: T(r,z)=(1/2)log(1+r^2)=log r+O(1), and the fixed rational composition law with the identity input gives T(r,f)=d log r+O(1) for a rational f of degree d, matching Goldberg-Ostrovskii Theorem 6.1 and (6.26) (Ch.1 Sec.6) and Eremenko Exercise 1. Reverse: chordal proximity is nonnegative so N(r,infinity;f)<=T(r,f)<=A log r; if the poles were infinite, choosing M>max{A,n(0)} and the least integer radius R_M carrying M counted poles gives N(R)>=M log R-(M-n_0)log R_M, contradicting the bound as R->infinity; hence finitely many poles, and q=prod(z-p_j)^{m_j} (q=1 if none) makes g=qf entire. T(r,q)=O(log r), the product law gives T(r,g)=O(log r), and T_0(r,g)<=T(r,g). The entire maximum-modulus inequality with R=2r gives M(r,g)<=C r^B; Cauchy estimates make every Taylor coefficient of index >B vanish, so the entire Taylor series makes g a polynomial and f=g/q rational. Empty pole set, a centre pole, a boundary pole and the constant-g branch are all handled; only finite enumeration and well-ordering of the integers are used, no AC. Sources for the reverse argument: Goldberg-Ostrovskii Ch.1 Sec.6-7, read with the log^+ characteristic whose difference from the chordal one is the bounded term controlled by the elementary-laws item.
